notes: Warehouse fire liability appeal; pleading and contribution issues are dense but the Court of Appeal's disposition is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Warehouse fire appeal: pleading, contribution and welding blanket liability
key_facts: A warehouse fire at Deeside Industrial Estate in May 2001 destroyed Re-source America's stored materials after hotwork by sub-sub-contractor Platt ignited combustible stock.
The TCC held Platt liable to Re-source but entitled to full indemnity or 100% contribution from main contractor Barkin for inadequate fire protection during steelwork.

The appeal turned on whether welding blankets were in place, whether Platt could pass liability to Barkin on a 'holes' basis raised late at trial, and whether Barkin's 100% contribution assessment was justified.
Barkin had rushed hotwork in Re-source's occupied warehouse without proper risk assessments after the tenant refused access until safety documents were provided.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a Technology and Construction Court trial of liability and Part 20 contribution/indemnity claims.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Barkin remained liable to indemnify Platt or contribute 100% for Re-source's fire damage, though Platt could not recover under Barkin's indemnity letter because holed blankets did not satisfy its conditions.
enrichment.ratio: A defendant may run a broad Part 20 case that a principal contractor assumed entire responsibility for fire protection where the pleadings and conduct at trial support it; late reliance on holes in welding blankets did not unfairly prejudice Barkin; and under section 2 of the Civil Liability (Contribution) Act 1978 a trial judge's 100% contribution assessment will stand unless clearly wrong, even where post-incident conduct is considered.
legal_issues: Whether the judge erred in finding welding blankets were in place at the final stanchion
Whether Platt could rely on holes in blankets against Barkin despite narrow pre-trial pleading
Whether Barkin was liable on contractual indemnity or contribution grounds
Whether the trial involved a serious procedural irregularity by deciding unpleaded issues

Canada Steamship Lines v King [1952] AC 192
McPhilemy v Times Newspapers Ltd (No 1) [1999] 3 All ER 775
Re-Source America International Ltd v Platt Site Services Ltd [2003] EWHC 1142 (TCC)

notes: GMC serious professional misconduct JR; PCC reasoning and Silver principles are fully analysed including costs and permission arguments.

enrichment.short_title: Judicial review of GMC finding of no serious professional misconduct
key_facts: Jennifer Campbell sought to quash a GMC Professional Conduct Committee decision clearing Dr Nigel Birkin of serious professional misconduct over substandard paediatric care of her son Michael and another child Amy Tasker on the Isle of Man.
The PCC found numerous acts of professional misconduct proved but concluded, after mitigation, that the threshold of serious professional misconduct was not met.
The claimant challenged the PCC's assessment of seriousness, its description of the cases as isolated incidents, and reliance on Dr Birkin's medical isolation on the Isle of Man.
Expert evidence had been highly critical of Dr Birkin's dangerous practice in managing hydrocephalus and head circumference monitoring.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for judicial review of a GMC Professional Conduct Committee decision; permission granted by Beatson J.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; permission to appeal refused; GMC awarded costs subject to public funding certificate confirmation.
enrichment.ratio: A PCC must consider all relevant circumstances, including mitigation, before deciding whether proved professional misconduct is serious; it need not make a separate discrete severity finding where it has already found the conduct capable of amounting to serious professional misconduct and then explained why mitigation prevailed; describing exceptional misconduct as isolated against an otherwise unblemished career is not necessarily perverse; and general reasons suffice for serious professional misconduct determinations.
legal_issues: Whether the PCC failed properly to assess the seriousness of proved misconduct
Whether describing protracted substandard care as isolated incidents was perverse
Whether reliance on medical isolation on the Isle of Man was irrational
Whether adequate reasons were given for finding no serious professional misconduct

notes: Wimbledon FC CVA challenge; section 4(4)(a) analysis and Sale Agreement facts are comprehensively reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Wimbledon FC CVA appeal on preferential creditor priority

statutes_considered.title: Transfer of Undertakings (Protection of Employment) Regulations 1981

key_facts: Wimbledon Football Club Ltd entered administration in June 2003 heavily insolvent, with Football League membership and player contracts as its main value.

Administrators proposed a CVA paying preferential creditors including the Inland Revenue about 30p in the pound from sale proceeds while a buyer would pay Football Creditors in full to retain League membership.
A Sale Agreement with Milton Keynes Dons Limited and Inter MK Limited was executed before creditor approval and required Football Creditors to be paid in full by the buyer from third-party funds.
The Revenue challenged approval of the voluntary arrangement under section 4(4)(a) because non-preferential Football Creditors would be paid ahead of preferential creditors.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Lightman J refusing the Inland Revenue's application to revoke or suspend approval of a company voluntary arrangement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the CVA did not infringe section 4(4)(a) because the Sale Agreement obligation to pay Football Creditors was not part of the creditors' proposal and involved third-party free money.
enrichment.ratio: Section 4(4)(a) of the Insolvency Act 1986 applies to a CVA proposal governing distribution of the company's assets, not to separate third-party payments made from the buyer's own money to preserve an asset without reducing consideration payable to the company; treating such payments as breaching preferential priority would undermine the flexibility of the CVA regime and preferential creditors cannot claim priority over unrelated third-party payments.
legal_issues: Whether payment of Football Creditors by the buyer infringed section 4(4)(a)
Whether the Sale Agreement formed part of the CVA proposal
Whether breach of section 4(4)(a) automatically invalidated approval or required revocation under section 6
Whether preferential creditors could avoid the arrangement by treating third-party creditor payments as company-funded

enrichment.short_title: GMC serious professional misconduct challenge over paediatric care failures
key_facts: The claimant sought to quash a GMC Professional Conduct Committee decision acquitting Dr Nigel Birkin of serious professional misconduct despite proved substandard care of Michael Boyle and Amy Tasker.
Findings included failure to monitor head circumference, delayed referrals, and inadequate supervision in hydrocephalus cases at Noble's Hospital, Isle of Man.
The PCC found the misconduct capable of being serious but concluded mitigation from 30 years of otherwise good practice meant serious professional misconduct was not established.
Challenges focused on failure to assess severity, use of the phrase isolated incidents, and reliance on medical isolation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a GMC Professional Conduct Committee decision following permission granted by Beatson J.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed on all three grounds of challenge.
enrichment.ratio: After findings of fact, a PCC must weigh all relevant circumstances including mitigation before deciding if misconduct is serious; a capability finding plus detailed criticism can show seriousness was considered without a separate discrete severity ruling; and general reasons are sufficient where the decision's basis is plain from the PCC's reasoning read with the findings.
legal_issues: Failure to assess seriousness of proved misconduct
Perverse description of misconduct as isolated incidents
Perverse reliance on medical isolation on the Isle of Man
Adequacy of reasons for acquittal on serious professional misconduct

enrichment.short_title: Confidential tender documents withheld in Network Rail procurement claim
key_facts: Express Medicals Ltd claimed Network Rail breached procurement transparency and equality obligations and an implied contract in awarding occupational healthcare contracts to Nationwide Healthcare Connections Ltd.
Network Rail disclosed tender documents with prices, staff names, client referees, and business plans redacted from successful competitor Healthcare's submissions.
Express Medicals sought inspection under CPR Part 31.19(5), arguing it needed identities and business plans to show Healthcare could not perform contracts matching the invitations to tender.
Healthcare intervened supporting further redactions to protect commercially confidential staff lists, client identities, and innovative service proposals.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for inspection of disclosed documents on a liability-only trial in procurement-related proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; existing and proposed obliterations upheld and three unredacted pricing passages ordered obliterated for the liability trial.
enrichment.ratio: Where confidential tender information is not necessary for a fair trial of whether contracts were awarded on materially different terms, inspection should be refused; a balancing exercise under CPR principles may weigh heavily in favour of preserving confidentiality in a competitive healthcare market, and requests to inspect staff identities and business plans were peripheral fishing expeditions on the pleaded case.
legal_issues: Whether CPR Part 31.19(5) applied without a formal withholding notice under paragraph (3)
Whether redacted staff, referee, and business plan information was necessary for fair disposal of liability
How confidentiality obligations in tender documents affected inspection
Whether obliterated material could support inference of contract variation

enrichment.short_title: Lawful development certificate refused for Bosham Hoe dwelling
key_facts: Trustees of the Stock Family trust sought certificates of lawfulness to build a further detached dwelling on land at Bosham Hoe near Chichester.
Historic 1949 and 1953 planning permissions for the Bosham Hoe Estate were implemented by construction of houses Lamorna and Brackendene on the appeal site.
An inspector refused certificates, construing the 1949 consent as outline permission for only one house on the combined plot and holding the 1953 consent did not cover red-shaded land.
The claimants challenged the inspector's interpretation under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 challenge to an inspector's decision refusing certificates of lawfulness of existing use or development.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; leave to appeal refused; Secretary of State awarded costs.
enrichment.ratio: A 1949 estate layout permission incorporated by reference to plans granting outline residential development on a single blue plot supports only one dwelling on that plot once implemented; construction of Lamorna and Brackendene exhausted that entitlement; and the 1953 permission, by reference to its plan distinguishing red sold plots from blue future building plots, did not extend to the appeal site.
legal_issues: Whether the 1953 consent covered land shown red on the application plan
Whether the 1949 consent permitted more than one house on plot C-D-E
Correct interpretation of historic planning permissions as outline consents
Whether the inspector erred in applying a one-house-per-plot convention

notes: Confession manslaughter retrial; Blastland third-party evidence ruling is the decisive issue and clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Manslaughter conviction quashed after exclusion of alternative suspect evidence
key_facts: Andrew Greenwood confessed in 1999 to killing Janet Murgatroyd in Preston in June 1996 after a chance encounter, having previously been unknown to police.
The Crown case at retrial depended entirely on detailed police interview confessions; psychiatric evidence explained possible false confession but did not make untruth more likely.
At the first trial the jury heard agreed facts about former boyfriend John Parkinson's violent history, proximity phone call, and forensic items; the jury could not agree.
At retrial Holland J excluded Parkinson evidence as irrelevant speculation, directing the jury to put Parkinson out of their minds, while allowing limited Hayes evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction for manslaughter by a majority verdict at retrial, with leave of the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction quashed as unsafe because exclusion of Parkinson motive and proximity evidence denied the defence material relevant to whether confessions were true.
enrichment.ratio: Where the prosecution case rests solely on confessions, a defendant must be permitted to adduce evidence pointing to another person's motive and possible involvement, including formal admissions about a former violent boyfriend investigated by police; excluding all Parkinson evidence while allowing some alternative-suspect material was inconsistent with Regina v Blastland and rendered the conviction unsafe in a finely balanced case.
legal_issues: Admissibility and relevance of third-party suspect evidence relating to John Parkinson
Whether exclusion of Parkinson evidence was a proper control of misleading evidence
Whether the manslaughter verdict was a compromise verdict
Whether jury pressure from holiday commitments affected the verdict
linked_authorities: Regina v Blastland [1986] 1 AC 41

confidence.notes: Appeal succeeds on a single clearly articulated evidential ruling; secondary grounds were rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Metro subcontract adjudication challenge over payment application 32

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996
Scheme for Construction Contracts (England and Wales) Regulations 1998

key_facts: Alstom Signalling Ltd subcontracted Jarvis Facilities Ltd for signalling and telecommunications on the Tyne and Wear Metro Sunderland Direct Project under an IChemE-based target cost subcontract.
Jarvis submitted payment application 32 including sums for a Jackson Eve Rail sub-sub-contract that Jarvis disputed and had not fully paid.
Adjudicator Mr Chapman decided the full application was payable, treating Alstom's queries as insufficient withholding notices under Schedule F.
Alstom sought declarations that the adjudicator erred and challenged Jarvis's summary judgment enforcement; Jarvis's information provision was partial and late.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court proceedings challenging an adjudicator's decision and opposing summary judgment enforcement.
enrichment.outcome: Declarations granted for Alstom that the adjudicator wrongly decided Alstom failed to issue a required withholding notice and that Jarvis was not entitled to payment for application 32, alternatively for disputed Eve Rail amounts; Jarvis's summary judgment application dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Under the subcontract payment regime an adjudicator must decide what is actually due when proper queries are raised, not simply pay the full application because Schedule F treats unsubstantiated applications as payable; a subcontractor cannot recover through adjudication amounts it does not accept and disputes, such as unpaid disputed sub-sub-contract claims included in the application.
legal_issues: Whether Alstom issued adequate withholding notices under Schedule F for application 32
Proper construction of neutral cash flow and payment application procedures
Whether the adjudicator should have quantified deductions for disputed sub-sub-contract sums
Whether Jarvis was entitled to summary judgment enforcing the adjudication decision

notes: International adoption after move to Scotland; section 13 home requirement analysis is the central legal issue and resolved in favour of adoption.

enrichment.short_title: Adoption allowed despite applicant's relocation to Scotland
key_facts: Ms H, an English expatriate, sought to adopt SL, a profoundly disabled boy abandoned in Hong Kong whom she had cared for since 1997.
Hong Kong authorities consented to adoption in the UK and placed SL with Ms H before she returned to London in October 2001.
Ms H issued her adoption application in England on 9 December 2003 but moved with SL to Scotland on 11 December 2003.
Local authority and guardian strongly supported adoption as plainly in SL's best interests.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Adoption application in the Principal Registry referred to a High Court judge because the applicant relocated to Scotland after issuing proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Adoption order made; English court had jurisdiction and section 13 requirements were satisfied despite the home moving from London to Scotland after application.
enrichment.ratio: Section 13(2) and section 13(3)(b) of the Adoption Act 1976 impose separate purposes: the 12-month home-with-applicant requirement tests placement stability and need not be the same home or be in England and Wales, while the section 13(3)(b) home environment inspection requirement applies only to the English or Welsh local authority area where notice was given under section 22(1).
legal_issues: Whether the English court retained jurisdiction after the applicant moved to Scotland
Whether section 13(2) required a continuous home in England for 12 months
Whether the section 13(2) and section 13(3)(b) homes must be the same
Whether Re Y prevented adoption where the home later moved outside England

notes: Complex medical treatment capacity case; interim declaration granted on incomplete expert evidence but reasoning is detailed and outcome clear.

enrichment.short_title: Interim declaration authorising blood transfusion despite advance directive
key_facts: Ms T, aged 37 with borderline personality disorder, repeatedly self-harmed by blood-letting causing life-threatening anaemia requiring emergency transfusions.
She signed an advance directive in January 2004 refusing blood transfusion and iron, partly because she believed her blood was evil.
In April 2004 Pauffley J made an out-of-hours declaration authorising transfusion when Ms T collapsed; she recovered after treatment.
Her treating psychiatrist Dr C considered she lacked capacity due to continuous disordered thinking, though other psychiatrists had disagreed in 2001.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 application for declaratory relief and interim declaration pending final hearing on lawfulness of future blood transfusions.
enrichment.outcome: Interim declaration granted that Ms T lacked capacity when signing the advance directive and that blood transfusion was lawful if medically necessary to preserve life or avoid imminent serious injury.
enrichment.ratio: An adult with borderline personality disorder whose refusal of life-saving transfusion is driven by a delusional belief that her blood is evil lacks capacity under Re MB; CPR Part 25.1 now permits interim declarations where, on present evidence, capacity is displaced and treatment is in best interests; and recurring emergency anaemia justified pragmatic interim relief pending fuller psychiatric evidence.
legal_issues: Whether Ms T had capacity when signing the advance directive
Whether she currently lacks capacity to refuse blood transfusion
True effect of the advance directive as binding refusal or consultation request
Jurisdiction and discretion to grant an interim declaration under CPR Part 25
